author: reek
body: Every line goes through `handle-console-input` in ModeDebug, and that is the point rather than a detail: `expr-eval` has its own test as a pure function, so what is left to prove is the WIRING -- that a line which is not a menu key reaches the evaluator, that a good one moves last-address, and that a bad one does not. Calling `expr-eval` directly here would pass against the arm that used to be `else state` and swallow the line, which is exactly the bug this closes.

author: reek
body: The last-address readings are the load-bearing ones. A status line can say anything; `$` is read back out of the state on the NEXT expression, so `$ + 16` proves the previous value was actually stored rather than printed and dropped.

author: reek
body: The refusal has to be checked the same way. After a bad expression the status changes -- so a test watching only the status would pass -- and what must NOT change is last-address. So the bad case is followed by a bare `$`, which reports what the cursor really is.

author: reek
body: The watch commands are here for the same reason and not to re-test `DevState`, which has its own test over memory it controls. What this half proves is that the console THREADS the returned table back into its own state: `watch.check` re-arms, and a dispatch that dropped the returned `DevState` would still print a plausible line while every later check reported against a stale snapshot. `armed-at-cursor` naming the address the expressions left behind is what ties the two features together -- the cursor an expression set is the region a watch arms on.
